title: Can you trust AI with complex money questions? Read three chatbots’ answers, rated by experts
html:
The Globe and Mail

Artificial intelligence chatbots can make expensive mistakes. They’ve invented tax rules, sent travellers on detours to made-up destinations and given iffy shopping advice. But they also learn fast.

Research by Stanford University, which tracks AI’s technical performance annually, shows models’ scores rising across language, reasoning and math. And as the bots improve, users report having long conversations with them about anything from debt management to their plans for retirement.

More than 50 per cent say they use AI for help with financial management, according to a recent TD survey, up from just 10 per cent last year.

But have AI agents truly become good enough for you to trust them with your money?

We put ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini to the test with two scenarios based on common financial dilemmas.

The first one asks whether to use a pay bonus for a mortgage down payment or a top-up to a registered retirement savings plan, or RRSP. In the second one, a fictional user wants to know how to navigate a layoff. Then we asked two financial advisers for their take.

Here are the main take-aways from what we learned. You can also read the scenarios and each bot’s full answer below, with annotations from the experts. (The Globe and Mail paraphrased some of the annotations for style and length.)

Chatbots have improved

If you asked chatbots a year ago how to save for a house or how to file taxes, you would have likely received advice based on information that had little to do with Canada.

“Even when you instructed it to only reference Canada, it didn’t always do that,” said Edmonton-based Chris Anderson, senior portfolio manager at Harbourfront Wealth, adding that models often leaned on U.S.-specific information.

In our two experiments, that is no longer an issue. When weighing whether to contribute to an RRSP or pay down a mortgage, for example, the chatbots correctly used tax rates for Ontario, where the fictional user in our first scenario is based.

Few factual errors

All three bots made relatively few factual errors.

“The hallucination issues are almost non-existent,” said Aravind Sithamparapillai, founder and financial planner at AMA Wealth Inc. in Hamilton.

“Tax rates were generally correct, income was generally correct, rates of return were not super far off.”

That said, there were still small mistakes. For example, in offering advice for managing money during a layoff, Gemini put the maximum employment insurance benefit rate in Canada at $668 per week, whereas the figure is currently up to $729-a-week or 55 per cent of average insurable earnings.

Not enough questions, plenty of assumptions

While the chatbots seem to have gotten better at delivering the facts based on the information provided, they didn’t probe much beyond the surface.

In our first scenario, for instance, all of the bots assumed that the bonus amount we provided was net of taxes, instead of asking for more information.

Claude also assumed a 25-year mortgage amortization before confirming it, adding that it was the “standard default for Canadian mortgages” and that the number happened to line up with the individual’s age.

If they don’t line up with reality, those assumptions can lead the bots off course, skewing the entire analysis and producing recommendations that don’t match the user’s situation. Harbourfront Wealth’s Mr. Anderson warned.

Also, the bots paid no mind to economic conditions that could influence the best course of action for a user. In our layoff scenario, they advised the user to look into mortgage renewal options early but did not mention that rates are currently rising for both fixed and variable rate mortgages.

An adviser would want to know, “Where is your rate going to go?” said Mr. Anderson.

Trouble connecting the dots

The bots also did a poor job of recognizing how specific financial choices would trickle down to other aspects of a user’s financial situation.

Weighing the benefits of an RRSP contribution versus a mortgage lump-sum payment, none of the bots asked about kids, even though considerations around the federal Canada Child Benefit should have factored into the analysis, according to Mr. Sithamparapillai.

Someone also getting a sizable pay bonus in addition to a $105,000 income might find themself in the highest tax rate that they will ever be at, Mr. Sithamparapillai said. If the household was previously eligible for the child benefit, using the bonus for a mortgage lump-sum payment could trigger a benefit reduction, tilting the scales heavily in favour of the RRSP contributions, he said.

Who came out on top?

Here’s how the advisers ranked the bots overall:

Third place: Gemini

Overall, Gemini came in last on our list because it had the most untested assumptions and was most emphatic in recommending a specific course of action based on incomplete information.

“It just didn’t ask enough questions.”

Second place: Claude

In the layoff scenario, Claude was the only bot that reminded the user to look at legal considerations and see whether she might be entitled to more severance pay from her former employer, Mr. Anderson noted.

“It focused on the client’s real problems: survival and flexibility during an uncertain employment period, rather than just optimizing the numbers,” he said.

It also paid attention to the possibility of an extended period of unemployment, weighing what that meant for a person’s financial security, AMA Wealth’s Mr. Sithamparapillai said.

On the other hand, the bot showed some big leaps in judgment in our first scenario, which docked it a few points. The fact that it assumed that the user had a 25-year mortgage amortization led it to draw conclusions on interest costs, disposable income and financial trade-offs that would have been incorrect if the user had a different amortization, Mr. Anderson said.

First place: ChatGPT

ChatGPT also had its fair share of untested assumptions but took the first spot because both advisers said the answers it provided came closest to the ones they might have given and attempted to ask reasonable follow-up questions.

Still, ChatGPT had a tendency to overload the user with information rather than zeroing in on what mattered most.

“The right answers, they’re kind of buried in a sea of noise,” Mr. Sithamparapillai said.

The upshot

AI chatbots are getting better at answering personal finance questions.

Where the tools still fall behind is in pinpointing the small but important details that get missed, and in asking the right questions to get them, Mr. Anderson said.

If you want to use AI to tackle personal finance questions, Mr. Sithamparapillai suggests providing as much detail as possible and specifically prompting the tool to ask you questions.

Try a question such as, “I’m trying to understand my current tax situation – what information should I be pulling together to form an accurate picture about this?” Mr. Sithamparapillai said.

Once the bot has provided its answer, ask it to show you its work, Mr. Sithamparapillai said. “Show me the article that references this, or show me a tax lawyer’s blog, explain this.”
summary: Have agents truly become good enough for you to rely on them for financial advice?
